newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK consumers, companies to gain from EMU- ABN Amro.
newsitem.headline: HK consumers, companies to gain from EMU- ABN Amro.

text.p: Hong Kong consumers and companies are likely to benefit from European monetary union, David Wong, assistant general manager and treasurer of ABN Amro in Hong Kong believes.
Increased competition among European companies will depress the prices of goods and services, while the existence of one currency rather than many will lower transaction costs, he said.

"Consumers will find it cheaper to travel and when ordering goods. As the market becomes more transparent, there will be increased competition that will place downward pressure on prices," Wong told a club meeting in Hong Kong.

Corporations will benefit from reduced foreign exchange hedging costs because they will need to hedge against one currency rather than many. Monetary convergence is likely to push down interest rates in Europe, which will allow companies here to raise funds cheaper in Europe, Wong said.
Hong Kong companies also will be able to cut costs by centralizing their treasury management in Europe, he said.

"Hong Kong companies will also find that there will be reasonably priced investment opportunities" spawned by increased merger ane acquisition activities in Europe and companies face tougher competition, Wong said.
But Hong Kong banks operating in Europe will face the same difficulties as European banks, which must contend with a loss of foreign exchange income, a loss of fee income and greater competition.

At present, Luxembourg is the only country that meets the criteria for joining the EMU, but Wong said he expects many other countries will either meet the criteria -- or come close enough to meeting the criteria -- by 1999, when monetary union is scheduled to become a reality.
"The criteria are guidelines principally, not commandments," he remarked.
Wong predicted that Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg, Austria, Finland, Ireland and possibly Portugal and Spain will be ready to join the group in 1999.

In the months leading up to 1999, those countries that are furthest away from meeting EMU criteria, such as Italy and Spain, will see the most volatility in their currencies, while those countries that are closest to meeting the qualifications will find their currencies strengthening, Wong said.
But the U.S. dollar will be the biggest beneficiary of the currency volatility ahead of 1999 as investors transfer cash to U.S. assets as a safe-haven move, he said.

After 1999, the strength of the Euro, the single European currency, will depend on the European Central Bank's ability to maintain economic discipline among member countries as well as on the Euro's role as a reserve currency.

Wong said he expects the U.S. dollar to remain the world's favored reserve currency, with 50 percent of international reserves held in dollars, 35 percent held in Euros and the remainder split between the Japanese yen and other currencies.
